title: Why Men and Angels Hailed Him King
english: Just as the boundless deep pours out the springs of water without stint, and the springs in turn let loose rivers that nothing can hold back, and the rivers visit the earth and drench it (Psalm 65:9) so that it bears bread for food and wine for the gladness of men (Psalm 104:14–15), and men, enjoying them, fulfill what is written, “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and those who seek Him shall praise the Lord” (Psalm 22:26): so too the unspeakable love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, out of the boundless deep of His goodness and love for mankind, makes His holy feasts spring up for us, the feasts in which He worked our salvation.

He Himself makes the feast spring up, and the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is at work in the feast, fills “the streams of the river”, by which I mean the God-bearing men who possess “teaching in teaching” (Romans 12:7). They in turn visit the earth of mankind, an earth of mind and reason, and gladden the holy Church, which is “the city of the great King” (Psalm 48:2), Jesus Christ, as it is written: “The streams of the river make glad the city of God” (Psalm 46:4). And the Church, gladdened and delighted out of the richness of her heart, praises and glorifies the Lord who reigns in her.

Come, then, today too let us speak of what He Himself proclaimed beforehand about Himself through His holy prophets. Let us search out, as far as we are able, the salvation that our King accomplished for us in this feast. Come, let us consider why not only men but the angelic powers too hymned Him as King.

The cause of the hymn, then, as it appears outwardly, was the raising of Lazarus, as the Gospel says: “But they took counsel to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus” (John 12:10–11). This is the outward cause of the believers’ praise; but its hidden and secret cause is the raising of the whole of human nature.

And just as the sign of Lazarus and that raising made men sing hymns to Jesus, so the sign of the raising of the whole of human nature led the holy angels to give glory; and as much greater as the raising of all is than the raising of Lazarus, so much greater was the glory then. The minds of those who shouted, astonished at the miracle, moved them to give glory; but the divine plan, on account of the raising of the whole of human nature, secretly moved not only men but also the holy angels to marvel at Jesus and glorify Him.

For the angelic powers saw, truly they saw, and learned, and were made wise with a wisdom they had not known: the wisdom made manifest from God, who created all things, through the Church of the faithful, the wisdom hidden in Him before the ages (Ephesians 3:9; 1 Corinthians 2:7). I mean the wisdom of the teachings, the promises, and the miracles of the Lord Jesus, as the inspired Paul says somewhere: “so that the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and the authorities through the Church” (Ephesians 3:10).

For the powers above are learning what they had never yet seen or heard. They are creatures, and there is no creature that has no need to learn; nor do they know what is going to happen, unless they are initiated into it by the holy, revered, and worshipful Trinity.

So they learned, and were made certain of, the resurrection of Adam when they saw the Lord raise the widow’s son (Luke 7:12–15); for the earth became like a widow when her son, the first-formed man, died. And when they saw Him raise the daughter of the synagogue ruler (Luke 8:49–55), they were made wise to know that He will raise Eve too, together with Adam. Again, when He raised up the servant of the foreign centurion (Matthew 8:5–13), they were also taught…
translator_notes: The Greek heading (“Hesychius, priest of Jerusalem, a discourse on Lazarus and on the palm branches”) and the edition’s Latin title line repeat the book title and are not translated. The edition notes that the homily was once credited to Titus of Bostra.
“The streams of the river” (Psalm 46:4) renders the Septuagint’s own word in that verse; Hesychius quotes the Psalm as the Septuagint has it.
Psalm numbers follow the English Bible. In the Septuagint, Psalm 65:9 is 64:10, Psalm 104:14–15 is 103:14–15, Psalm 22:26 is 21:27, Psalm 48:2 is 47:3, and Psalm 46:4 is 45:5.
“Teaching in teaching” takes up Paul’s words about the one who teaches, “in teaching” (Romans 12:7).
Hesychius counts the centurion’s servant (Matthew 8:5–13) with the widow’s son and the synagogue ruler’s daughter as the three raised from the dead, although the Gospel tells of a healing.
The last sentence runs on into the next section: “they were also taught… this: that He will raise even the foreign nations.”
